subject: radiology
title: Contrast safety: kidneys and allergy

steps.tx: Contrast can injure the kidney, and danger grows when kidney function already stays poor. **Contrast associated kidney injury** becomes more likely when the patient stays dehydrated or receives a large contrast load. The team protects a high risk kidney with **pre hydration using isotonic fluids** before and after the contrast reaches the kidney. A patient who takes **metformin** needs careful review because the drug pauses when the kidney may fail. The team splits a large load across **staged procedures** when one sitting would overwhelm the kidney.
steps.say: Contrast can injure the kidney and the danger grows when kidney function already stays poor. The injury becomes more likely when the patient stays dehydrated or receives a large contrast load. The team keeps a high risk kidney safe with isotonic fluids before and after the injection. A patient who takes metformin needs careful review because the drug pauses when the kidney may fail. The team splits a large load across separate sittings when one sitting would overwhelm the kidney.

steps.tx: This illustration is helpful because it shows a kidney that receives a large dye load while the medulla narrows its small vessels. The inset magnifies the **renal tubules**, where concentrated dye and poor flow injure the lining cells. The drip beside the kidney shows **isotonic pre hydration**, which dilutes the dye and keeps urine flowing through the tubules. The picture matters for the exam because prior impairment, dehydration and large loads raise risk together. Hydration before the study remains the main protection that the team can offer.

steps.tx: A contrast reaction can start suddenly, so the team asks carefully about every previous reaction before giving contrast. A **prior contrast reaction** predicts another reaction and the patient then needs steroid cover before an elective study. The lab stays ready for **anaphylaxis** at all times, with adrenaline drawn and staff who rehearse the emergency drill. Elective cover starts hours before the dye because oral steroids need time to work properly. A patient with a severe previous reaction may need **alternative imaging** with ultrasound or carbon dioxide instead of iodinated contrast.

steps.tx: Contrast also affects organs beyond the kidney, and the examiner expects those wider harms in a complete answer. Iodine load can rarely trigger a **thyroid storm** when hyperthyroidism stays uncontrolled before the study begins. A large osmotic load can worsen **heart failure**, so the team injects slowly and watches the breathing closely. Metformin becomes dangerous when the kidney fails, because retained drug can lead toward **lactic acidosis** over time. A **delayed skin rash** can appear days later and usually settles with antihistamines and simple reassurance for the patient.

steps.tx: Good records prevent the same contrast harm from happening again at the next hospital visit. The team flags a reactor with an **allergy band** and clear notes that follow the patient across every encounter. Staff also record the **dye volume** for each study so cumulative load stays visible across staged work. A high risk patient needs a **creatinine recheck** after the study because early detection allows early treatment of kidney injury. The patient leaves with a **patient card** that states the reaction clearly for the next clinical team.
